title: Arabic grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is Modern Standard Arabic, fully vowelled, with a reading in Latin letters.

units.title: Numbers, time and more than one

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Arabic conversation.

goal.t: مَرْحَبًا، أَنَا سَارَةُ. أَنَا مِنْ كَنَدَا.
goal.r: marḥaban, anā sāratu. anā min kanadā.
goal.tr: Hello, I'm Sarah. I'm from Canada.

blocks.p: Look at what is missing in this conversation: Arabic has no word for “am”, “is” or “are” in the present. {{أَنَا سَارَةُ}} is, word for word, “I Sarah”. You simply put the two side by side.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Egypt.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.

blocks.p: **I and you.** {{أَنَا|anā}} is “I”, for a man or a woman. “You” depends on who you're talking to: {{أَنْتَ|anta}} to a man, {{أَنْتِ|anti}} to a woman. Karim says {{مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟}} to Sarah, and she answers {{وَأَنْتَ؟}} “and you?”.

**Asking.** The question word comes first: {{مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ؟|min ayna anta?}} “Where are you from?”, word for word “from where you?”. And {{وَأَنْتِ؟|wa-anti?}} “and you?” turns any question back to the other person.

ex.note: said by a woman: the ending {{ة}} makes words feminine (a later lesson)
a question just by raising your voice

blocks.tip: The small marks above and below the letters are the vowels (a, i, u): the next lesson shows how to read them. Until then, the reading in Latin letters tells you how to say each example, and tapping an example lets you hear it.

mistakes.why: There is no “am” in the present: put {{أَنَا}} and the word side by side.
Sarah is a woman, so “you” is {{أَنْتِ}}, anti.

practice.q: You're talking to a woman. “You” is…
practice.why: {{أَنْتِ}}, anti, is for a woman; {{أَنْتَ}}, anta, for a man.

practice.q: You're Sami, from Jordan. Choose your replies.

lines.why: About yourself: {{أَنَا}}. (Jordan is “the Jordan” in Arabic: {{الْأُرْدُنُّ}}.)

practice.q: Ask a man: “Where are you from?”
Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{مَرْحَبًا، أَنَا…}}

answers.t: مَرْحَبًا، أَنَا جُون. أَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِيكَا.
answers.r: marḥaban, anā jūn. anā min amrīkā.
answers.tr: Hello, I'm John. I'm from America.

answers.t: أَهْلًا، أَنَا مَارِيَا. أَنَا مِنْ إِسْبَانِيَا.
answers.r: ahlan, anā māriyā. anā min isbāniyā.
answers.tr: Hi, I'm Maria. I'm from Spain.

lessons.title: Say what you want
lessons.summary: Ask for things, and say what you want to do: “I want to learn Arabic.”
lessons.topic: {{أُرِيدُ}} with a noun; {{أَنْ}} and the -a form of a verb (the subjunctive)

dialog.t: لَا، شُكْرًا. وَأُرِيدُ أَنْ أَدْفَعَ الْآنَ.
dialog.r: lā, shukran. wa-urīdu an adfaʿa l-āna.
dialog.tr: No, thanks. And I'd like to pay now.

blocks.p: **Wanting a thing.** {{أُرِيدُ|urīdu}} “I want”, then what you want: {{أُرِيدُ قَهْوَةً.}} “I want a coffee.” The thing you want ends in -an here ({{قَهْوَةً|qahwatan}}, {{مَاءً|māʾan}} “water”, {{شَايًا|shāyan}} “tea”); a later lesson explains that ending, so for now just copy it.

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: write, go, learn, want.

blocks.p: **Wanting to do something.** Put {{أَنْ|an}} “to” between {{أُرِيدُ}} and the second verb. Compare:

table: {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَتَعَلَّمَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ.|urīdu an ataʿallama l-ʿarabiyyata.}}

blocks.p: Two things change. {{أَنْ}} comes in, and the verb's last vowel turns from -u into -a: {{أَتَعَلَّمُ}} becomes {{أَنْ أَتَعَلَّمَ}}. And both verbs say who: {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ}} is, word for word, “I want that I go”.

blocks.means: a form of a verb used after certain little words, such as {{أَنْ}} “to”. In Arabic, the verb then ends in -a instead of -u.

ex.tr: I'd like a room for one night.
What do you want to eat?

blocks.tip: {{أُرِيدُ}} is polite enough in a shop or a café. Add {{مِنْ فَضْلِكَ|min faḍlika}} “please” (to a woman: {{مِنْ فَضْلِكِ|min faḍliki}}).

mistakes.why: Two verbs need {{أَنْ}} between them, and the second one ends in -a.
After {{أَنْ}}, the verb ends in -a, not -u.

practice.q: Which one means “I want to understand”?
practice.why: {{أَنْ}}, and the verb after it ends in -a.

practice.q: At the café: choose your replies.

lines.why: {{أُرِيدُ}} and what you want. ({{أَنَا شَايٌ}} would be “I am tea”!)

practice.q: How do you say “I want to learn Arabic”?
Your turn: what do you want to learn, and where do you want to go this year? Answer with {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ…}}

answers.tr: I want to go to Morocco.

answers.t: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَتَكَلَّمَ مَعَ أَصْدِقَائِي بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ.
answers.r: urīdu an atakallama maʿa aṣdiqāʾī bi-l-ʿarabiyyati.
answers.tr: I want to talk to my friends in Arabic.
